title: Anticipatory burst slots and preemptive shedding for Dedicated fleets
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Dedicated fleets occasionally see short, high-intensity bursts of requests from a single customer or route that temporarily saturate a pool and cause tail latency spikes or dropped requests for other tenants. Existing admission controls provide long-term fairness but do not smoothly absorb short bursts without either (a) over-reserving capacity which raises cost, or (b) aggressive shedding that degrades latency for the bursting customer.

Goal: Implement an anticipatory burst-slot mechanism combined with a preemptive shedding policy that: (1) allows controlled, temporary burst capacity to preserve latency for short spikes, (2) guarantees long-term throughput fairness across customers, and (3) gracefully sheds work when the fleet or pool approaches sustained overload.

Scope: Work covers router-side admission logic, dedicated fleet admission controller, and metrics/dashboarding for rollout. Does NOT include quantization/runtime changes or billing integration (separate ticket).

Design proposal (high level):
- Burst slots: allocate a small number of transient 'burst slots' per pool that can be borrowed by routes when they see short spike patterns (burst defined by request-rate acceleration over short windows). Slots are funded by slack capacity: we compute expected headroom per pool using the 95th percentile steady-state utilization and hold N slots per pool where N is a function of recent utilization variance.
- Anticipatory detection: augment router to detect acceleration (e.g., 2x rate increase within 10s) and mark requests as "burst-eligible" for a TTL (e.g., 30s). Burst-eligible requests can consume burst slots if available and bypass some normal admission queuing for a short path.
- Preemptive shedding: if pool utilization exceeds sustained threshold (e.g., 85% over 60s) and burst slots are depleted, start preemptive shedding by (a) routing new burst-eligible requests to lower-cost model variants or fallbacks, then (b) degrading request concurrency for low-priority routes and eventually (c) rejecting non-SLA traffic. Shedding decisions should be weighted by route priority and historical SLA commitments.
- Fairness reclamation: when bursts end, occupancy from burst slots reverts to pool slack. If a customer consistently uses burst slots beyond a configured quota window (e.g., 5m), throttle them to protect guarantees or require upgrade to a higher tier.

Trade-offs and considerations:
- Complexity vs predictability: anticipatory detection improves short-burst experience but adds complexity to routing logic and metrics. We favor conservative heuristics initially with a plan to evolve to ML-based burst predictors.
- Cost vs latency: burst slots increase short-term utilization and may raise unit cost slightly but should reduce error/latency incidents. Document expected trade-offs in the rollout notes.
- Safety: all new admission paths must be fenced behind feature flags and have observability before any user-facing rollout.

Instrumentation & metrics:
- Burst slot allocation and consumption per pool (timeseries)
- Burst-eligible request counts, route-level burst acceptance rate
- Preemptive shed events and reason codes
- Tail latency (p50/p95/p99) correlated with burst events
- Fairness delta metrics: per-customer throughput vs guaranteed baseline

Rollout plan:
1) Canary build (internal pools only) with flag off for public tenants. Monitor metrics for 2 weeks.
2) Soft enable for a small percentage of dedicated pools (5%), observe fairness and cost indicators for 1 week.
3) Ramp to 25% with opt-in for customers who want better burst experience.
4) Full enable with default conservative quotas and opt-out available.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for allocation math and heuristics
- Integration tests using the dedicated pool simulator (synthetic bursts, slow-draining queues)
- Chaos testing: simulate partial pool failures while bursts active
- End-to-end canary traffic with production-like patterns

Security and compliance: no new customer data paths. Admission decisions are metadata-only. Continue to route audit logs to existing audit pipeline.

Artifacts and references:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Anticipatory+Burst+Slots+Design
- Simulator PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/inference-sim/pull/412
- Router prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/router/pull/1287
- Observability dashboard draft: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/9a7b/anticipatory-burst-slots
acceptance_criteria: Router exposes a feature-flagged anticipatory burst detection path and burst-eligible request header
Pools report burst slot allocation and consumption metrics to telemetry pipeline
Preemptive shedding decisions generate clear reason codes and are reversible via config
Integration tests show <2% additional 95th latency during 10s synthetic bursts when burst slots are enabled (compared to baseline) and no sustained fairness regressions over 30m windows
Canary rollout plan executed with metric thresholds and rollback documented
